title: Goblin Gold

beats.text: The first book about the stock market says your profits are goblin treasure.
Amsterdam, sixteen eighty-eight. Joseph de la Vega writes it as a conversation about East India Company shares.
Imagine you're the shareholder: shares climb, you're a king; they fall, you're ruined.
So what advice does the book give?
Rule one: never give anyone advice to buy or sell.
Rule two: take your gain, don't mourn the profit you missed.
Rule three: profits on the exchange are goblin treasure.
Red jewels, then coal, diamonds, pebbles, morning dew, then tears.
You see, it's like checking your bank app ten times a day: nothing you own changed, only the number did.
And while he was still writing, the market crashed.
Rule four: to win this game, you need two things.

facts.claim: Confusion de Confusiones (Confusión de Confusiones), by Joseph (Penso) de la Vega, Amsterdam 1688, written in Spanish, is the first/earliest known book about a stock exchange
De la Vega was a merchant
Written as dialogues among a philosopher, a merchant and a shareholder (four dialogues)
The trading discussed is mostly in Dutch East India Company (VOC) shares
First principle: never give anyone the advice to buy or sell shares
Second principle: take every gain without showing remorse about missed profits
Third principle: profits on the exchange are the treasures of goblins - carbuncle stones (red gems), then coals, then diamonds, then flint-stones/pebbles, then morning dew, then tears
Fourth principle: whoever wishes to win in this game must have patience and money
A crisis/crash hit the Amsterdam market in 1688 while the author was still writing the book

caption:
Amsterdam, 1688: Joseph de la Vega wrote the first book ever about the stock market, Confusion of Confusions.
His third rule: profits on the exchange are goblin treasure. Jewels, then coal, then diamonds, then tears.
His fourth: patience and money.
